# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga & Holm's Comment on the Halden Pilot

Most of this comment is valuable. Using the microdata, it documents problems that could only be suspected from the working paper:
- **Attrition was misdescribed.** Seven of the nine withdrawals came *after* the reduced schedule began, and most cited workload, not scheduling. This contradicts the working paper's account and is a significant finding in its own right.
- **Manager ratings overstate output.** In 19 of the 23 organisations that submitted records, the manager's index was higher than the record-based one.
- **Actual hours fell by only about 14%, not 20%.**
- **Real revenue fell.** The working paper reported nominal revenue.

Most of the arithmetic checks out:
- 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6% and 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- The hours ratios of 0.859 and 0.861 are correct.
- 1.014/1.041 is a real revenue change of −2.6%.

The weakness is that the conclusion goes well beyond the evidence. Sections 1–5 support "the Halden gain was overstated by more than half." Sections 6–8 claim that per-hour gains from reduced-hours schemes in general are "entirely an artifact." The data don't support that, and the comment's own preferred evidence contradicts it.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the randomised evidence the comment relies on

Section 5 calls the Varden counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." But the same trial's case-processing stratum found output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4). Every correction the comment recommends was already built into that estimate:
- **Selection** is addressed by randomisation and a control group.
- **Output** comes from administrative records, not managers.
- **Hours** are actual hours from timesheets.

Varden's counter stratum also showed +6.7% per actual hour, although I'd attribute much of that to busier staff with less idle time. Of the comment's four explanations, only novelty could account for Varden's case-processing gain, and that trial ran nine months rather than six.

The comment can't treat Varden as the most reliable evidence on coverage-bound work while leaving its knowledge-work result out of a conclusion that the gains are "entirely an artifact." A defensible conclusion would be: the Halden gain is substantially overstated; the randomised evidence suggests a real but smaller per-hour gain in non-coverage work; and durability is unknown.

The conclusion also covers "reduced-hours schemes" in general, when the comment re-analyses only one pilot.

## 2. Table 2 mixes the effect of each correction with changes in which organisations are counted

Each row uses a different set of organisations (61, 23, 27 and 17). The drop from 23.4% to 10.8% is therefore partly the corrections and partly a change in sample composition. The abstract's statement "the gain falls from 23.4% to 10.8%" compares a 61-organisation figure with a 17-organisation figure.

The data note acknowledges this, but Table 2 is still presented as "successive corrections." The fix is simple: compute all four specifications on the 17 organisations that have both records and time tracking. That would show how much each correction contributes on the same sample.

## 3. Attrition is described but not corrected

The abstract says the gain falls to 10.8% after "correcting the first three" problems, which include attrition. Table 2 does not correct for attrition at all; all of its subsets contain only organisations that completed the pilot. The comment shows that attrition was non-random but never quantifies its effect.

Since seven withdrawing organisations ran the schedule for one to two months, the microdata may contain their early monthly output indexes. Possible approaches:
- An estimate that keeps the withdrawers in the sample, using their last observed values (an intention-to-treat estimate).
- Bounds on the effect, for example by assigning withdrawers pessimistic or optimistic outcomes.

Either would turn a qualitative point into a correction. As written, the abstract overstates what was done.

## 4. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

Section 3 says the extra time comes from +0.7 hours per day on four days plus 1.6 hours on the day off. That totals 4.4 hours on top of a 32-hour schedule:
- 32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = **36.4 hours**
- If the +0.7 is measured against the baseline day of about 8.06 hours, the total is about 36.6 hours.

The reported pilot average is **34.6 hours**, about two hours lower. Either the breakdown or the total is wrong. This matters for the result: if actual hours were really around 36.4, the hours reduction is about 10%, not 14%, and the per-hour gain shrinks further. Possible explanations include an unweighted versus weighted average, organisations without a four-day pattern, or part-time staff. The authors need to reconcile the figures.

## 5. The novelty argument is speculative and skips the direct test

- **The extrapolation is from two points and is miscalculated.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD between months three and six, about 0.107 per month. A linear extrapolation reaches zero at about month **8.7**, not "around month ten." Fitting a straight line to two points is also unjustified; energy may level off rather than keep falling.
- **Energy is not output.** A fall in self-reported energy doesn't show that productivity falls.
- **The direct test is available but unused.** The pilot collected output indexes monthly. The comment should plot output, or record-based output where available, by month. If novelty explains the gain, output per hour should decline over months three to six. That analysis would test the hypothesis instead of inferring it.
- **The burden-of-proof argument works against the comment.** If six months cannot distinguish novelty from a durable effect, it also cannot establish that the gain is "entirely" novelty.
- **Some mechanisms shouldn't fade with novelty.** Removing low-value meetings and reporting is a structural change, not extra effort.

## 6. The comment's account of the Varden meetings analysis is inaccurate

- **The offices were not a post hoc subgroup.** The seven offices are the treated case-processing stratum, which was defined before randomisation. They were not chosen after the results.
- **The data weren't collected after the results were known.** Varden collected meeting data in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- **Varden didn't present it as an established mechanism.** It said the reduction "may account for part of the gain." It stressed the n = 7 limitation and that the analysis was unregistered, and it registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up. The comment doesn't mention any of this.

It is fair to say the correlation is weak evidence: r = 0.71 with n = 7 has p ≈ 0.07. But that is what Varden itself said. The fair recommendation is "await the registered confirmatory test," not "should not be cited."

## 7. Smaller points

- **"Billable hours delivered" is a poor output measure for this purpose.** It is partly a measure of hours worked, so it falls almost automatically when hours are cut. Report results with and without these organisations.
- **Averaging may differ.** The working paper used employee-weighted means. State whether Table 1 is weighted the same way; otherwise 98.9 and 95.1 aren't directly comparable to 98.7.
- **The choice of price index matters.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue; sector output prices would be better. The direction of the conclusion is probably unaffected.
- **Revenue doesn't contribute to the corrected figure.** The abstract lists revenue among the "four problems [that] account for most of the reported gain," but revenue plays no part in the per-hour calculation.
- **Sick days are not addressed.** The comment doesn't mention the reported −36% fall, part of which is automatic because staff have fewer scheduled days on which to be absent. With fewer days, it would be about −20% even if the rate of sickness per working day had not changed.
- **Retail is a very small sample.** The −11.2% record-based retail figure rests on three organisations.

## Summary

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Withdrawals happened after the schedule started and were mostly workload-related | Well supported; an important correction to the working paper |
| Manager index overstates record-based output (~4 points) | Well supported; check the weighting and billable-hours cases |
| Actual hours fell ~14%, not 20% | Supported, but the hours breakdown doesn't add up (§4) |
| Corrected gain ≈ 10.8% | Plausible for the 17-organisation subset; not attrition-corrected; Table 2 mixes subsets |
| Real revenue fell ~2.6% | Correct arithmetic |
| Sector-general claim is an artifact | Well supported |
| Remaining gain is novelty | Speculative; the direct monthly test is available but not done |
| Meetings hypothesis is post hoc | Mischaracterises Varden's design and caveats |
| Per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" | Not supported; contradicted by Varden's case-processing result |

## Suggested revisions

1. Run every specification in Table 2 on the 17-organisation subset.
2. Add an attrition correction, or drop "correcting the first three" from the abstract.
3. Reconcile the hours breakdown with the 34.6-hour total.
4. Test novelty directly using the monthly output data.
5. Engage with Varden's case-processing result and describe its meetings analysis accurately.
6. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion matched to the evidence. For example: the Halden gain is overstated by more than half; per-hour gains in coverage-bound work are small and don't offset lost presence; and in other work, randomised evidence points to a real but modest gain whose durability is untested.

With those changes, this would be a strong and useful comment. Its empirical sections are the best evidence so far on what went wrong in the Halden pilot.
